title: Today the angels sing and Adam is renewed
english: Today the choirs of angels sing divine praises, and the light of Christ's coming dawns on the faithful. Today is a glad spring for us: Christ, the Sun of Righteousness (Malachi 4:2), has shone forth, has lit us all around with clear light, and has enlightened the minds of the faithful. Today Adam is made new, and, lifted up into heaven, he dances in the choirs with the angels. Today the whole world is full of joy at the coming of the Holy Spirit upon humankind. Today divine grace, the hope of things unseen, shines out, and makes plain to us the wonders that surpass mind and understanding and the mystery that was hidden from eternity.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 9, col. D, to p. 10, col. A (PDF pp. 33-34); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Divina gratia is the subject of both effulget and facit, and miracula and mysterium are both objects of palam facit: divine grace shines out and makes plain to us the wonders that surpass mind and understanding and the mystery hidden from eternity. 'sol iustitiae' = Malachi 4:2 in English Bibles (Malachi 3:20 in the Hebrew/Vulgate numbering), cited. 'spes invisibilium' may recall Romans 8:24-25 or Hebrews 11:1; uncertain, not cited. 'choros agit' rendered 'dances in the choirs' (chorus = choral dance). The illegible margin variant at 'renovatur' was not used.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 9, col. D, to p. 10, col. A (PDF pp. 33-34)

title: Sermo I opening: today's joy, David's oracle, and Gabriel's hail
english: Today crowns of everlasting virtue are woven. Today God, wishing to crown the sacred heads of the kind and the devout, and of those who keep the feast days with zeal, names the lovers of firm faith as those called and as heirs; and the kingdom above eagerly calls those who set their minds on heavenly things, so that they may join themselves to the divine ministry of the bodiless choirs.

Today the oracle of David is fulfilled, which says: Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult. The fields will be glad, and all the trees of the forest, before the Lord, for He comes (Psalm 96:11-13). David, for his part, speaks of trees; but the Forerunner of the Lord speaks of trees that bear fruit worthy of repentance (Matthew 3:8-10), or rather worthy of the Lord's coming. Yet our Lord Jesus Christ announces everlasting joy to all who believe in Him. For He says: I will see you, and you will rejoice; and your joy no one will take from you (John 16:22).

Today the renowned and ineffable mystery of the Christians, who have freely set a seal on their hope in Christ, is plainly announced to us. Today Gabriel, who stands before God (Luke 1:19), coming to the most chaste Virgin, announces to her that saying: Hail, full of grace (Luke 1:28). And as she was considering within herself what sort of greeting that was (Luke 1:29), the Angel at once added, saying: The Lord is with you (Luke 1:28). Do not fear, Mary; for you have found grace with God. Therefore you will conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they will call His name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give Him the throne of David His father, and He will reign in the house of Jacob forever; and of His kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:30-33).

Then Mary said to the Angel: How will this be done to me, since I do not know a man? (Luke 1:34) Shall I still remain a virgin? Will the dignity of virginity in me be betrayed and lost? While the most holy Virgin, as if in wonder, was turning these things over in her mind, the Angel briefly sets out the sum of his message and says: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. And therefore the holy one who will be born of you will also be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). For what He is, that He will also surely be called. Fittingly, then, grace chose holy Mary alone out of all generations.
notes_covered: Opera omnia, Greek and Latin (Paris, 1622), Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 10, cols. A-D (PDF p. 34); Greek column checked on the page image at two places
translator_notes: 'supernumque regnum ... vocat': the Latin allows the kingdom to be either subject or object; the facing Greek makes the kingdom above the subject, and the English follows it. 'Hodie celebre atque ineffabile Christianorum ... mysterium ... adnunciatur': the subject is the mystery. 'sacra ... capita' = 'the sacred heads'. Mary's two further questions after Luke 1:34 are Gregory's expansion, not Scripture. 'solam gratia elegit': grace is the subject of 'chose' (Greek 'he charis exelexato'). 'summa sermonis' = 'the sum of his message'. 'omnino' rendered 'surely'. The Psalm is 95 in the Latin numbering (print margin 'Psal. 95'), Psalm 96 in English Bibles. The Forerunner's 'trees bearing fruit worthy of repentance' is Matthew 3:8-10 (the print's margin reads 'Matth. 4'). 'qui Deo assistit' recalls Luke 1:19, and 'what sort of greeting that was' Luke 1:29. 'ex omnibus generationibus' may echo Luke 1:48; uncertain, not cited. Margin variants not adopted: 'al. ante faciem Domini', 'al. pie ac sancte obsignarunt', 'al. Ecce concipies', 'al. vocabis'.
source_ref: Opera omnia, Greek and Latin (Paris, 1622), Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 10, cols. A-D (PDF p. 34)

title: Mary's wisdom undoes Eve's fall
english: For she was truly prudent and wise in all things, and no woman like her has ever been found among all the generations. She was not like the virgin Eve of old, who, alone in paradise, dancing and leaping, with her mind slackened through carelessness, received the word from the serpent, the author of all evil (Genesis 3:1-6), and so was corrupted in the understanding of her mind; and through her the deceiver, pouring out his poison and mingling death with it, brought it into the whole world. From this all the affliction of the saints was born. But in the holy Virgin alone that fall was repaired.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 10, col. D, to p. 11, col. A (PDF pp. 34-35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'Non sicut antea virgo Eva ... verbum suscepit' contrasts Mary with Eve; Eve is the subject of suscepit, so it is rendered 'She was not like the virgin Eve of old, who ... received the word', without adding a second receiving by Mary. 'eius lapsus' is ambiguous (Eve's fall, or the fall brought in through her); rendered 'that fall' to keep the ambiguity. Genesis 3:1-6 cited for the serpent and Eve. 'sensu mentis corrupta' may echo 2 Corinthians 11:3 (Vulgate 'corrumpantur sensus vestri ... sicut serpens Evam seduxit'), and death brought into the world may echo Wisdom 2:24 or Romans 5:12; uncertain, not cited. Margin variants 'al. prima virgo' and 'al. mente cordis' not adopted. 'ulla' (feminine) rendered 'no woman'.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 10, col. D, to p. 11, col. A (PDF pp. 34-35)

title: The Virgin asks where the gift comes from
english: Nor did the most holy Virgin accept the gift before she had learned who was sending it, what the gift was, and who was bringing it. Speaking with herself as one in two minds, she said to the Angel: From where have you brought us such a blessing? From what treasuries has the pearl of the word been sent out to us? From where has the gift made ready its substance for us? You have come from heaven, yet you walk on earth; you show a human form, yet you shine with the brightness of light.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, cols. A-B (PDF p. 35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: The Virgin's questions are the author's expansion of the scene, not a Gospel quotation, so nothing is cited. 'Unde nobis donum materiam paravit?' is obscure (literally 'whence has the gift prepared matter for us?'); rendered close to the letter as 'made ready its substance'. The margin variant 'al. promissum' (perhaps 'promissum' for 'donum', 'the promise') was not adopted. 'addidicisset' as printed (from addisco). 'et ... resplendes' rendered 'yet you shine' to bring out the contrast set up by the previous clause.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, cols. A-B (PDF p. 35)

title: Gabriel answers: do not fear, grace is above nature
english: While the most holy Virgin was thinking these things over within herself, the Archangel settled her questioning with words like these, saying to her: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born of you will also be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). And do not fear, Mary: for I have not come to strike fear into you, but to drive the cause of fear away from you. Do not fear, Mary; for you have found grace with God (Luke 1:30). Do not judge grace by the measure of nature; for grace does not allow itself to be made subject to the laws of nature.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, cols. B-C (PDF p. 35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Ib. Luc. 1': Luke 1:35 and Luke 1:30. Section 1 renders 'gratiam apud Deum' as 'favor with God'; here 'grace with God' is used because the next two sentences play on gratia ('do not judge grace by nature'), and 'favor' would break the link. The first 'Et ne timeas Maria' opens the author's own expansion and is left uncited; the full clause 'Ne timeas Maria: invenisti enim gratiam apud Deum' carries the citation. Margin variant 'al. legi' (singular 'law') not adopted; it does not change the sense.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, cols. B-C (PDF p. 35)

title: Mysteries hidden from prophets and angels made known to her
english: You know, Mary, what was hidden from the patriarchs and prophets. You have learned, O Virgin, what until now was hidden even from the angels. You have heard, most holy one, what the choir of those inspired by the divine Spirit was never found worthy to hear. Moses and David, Isaiah and Daniel, and all the prophets foretold Him, but they did not know the manner or the reason. But you alone, most holy Virgin, now receive the mysteries that were unknown to all of them, and you understand their cause. For where the Holy Spirit is, all things are brought to completion readily and without delay. Where divine grace is present, all things are possible with God (Luke 1:37; Matthew 19:26).
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, cols. C-D (PDF p. 35); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'omnia Deo sunt possibilia': the wording matches Matthew 19:26 / Mark 10:27, while the Annunciation context points to the angel's word in Luke 1:37; both cited inline, Mark 10:27 left in this note. 'Quae adhuc Angelis etiam fuerunt abscondita' may recall 1 Peter 1:12 or Ephesians 3:9-10; uncertain, not cited. 'divino spiritu afflatorum chorus' rendered 'the choir of those inspired by the divine Spirit' (the inspired prophets; 'divino spiritu' kept, capitalised because it is the Spirit of God). Margin variant 'al. suscipe et intellige' (imperatives: 'receive and understand') not adopted; the print's indicatives fit 'nunc' and the run of the passage.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, cols. C-D (PDF p. 35)

title: The Son of God, the ever-living fountain of light
english: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born of you will also be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). But if He is the Son of God, He is also God, of the same form as the Father and coeternal with Him. In Him the Father possesses all glory; He is, in His own person, the imprint and the image, and through the radiance the glory shines out (Hebrews 1:3).

And as rivers flow from an ever-flowing spring, so from this ever-flowing and ever-living spring comes forth the everlasting and true Light of the world, Christ our God (John 1:9; John 8:12). For of Him the prophets cried out: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God (Psalm 46:4). And not one city only, but all; for it gladdens the whole world as though it were one city.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 11, col. D, to p. 12, col. A (PDF pp. 35-36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 45' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 45:5 = Psalm 46:4 in English Bibles; English numbering used in the citation. 'character atque imago in persona ... per splendorem gloria' reflects Hebrews 1:3 (Greek charakter tes hypostaseos, apaugasma tes doxes); cited. 'imago' may also recall Colossians 1:15 and 'eiusdem formae' Philippians 2:6; not cited separately. 'clarificatio' rendered 'glory'. 'in persona' rendered 'in His own person' rather than 'of His person', which would import Hebrews 1:3 wording the Latin does not have; 'per splendorem gloria refulget' kept as 'through the radiance the glory shines out' (no added 'through Him, as'). 'vera lux mundi' joins John 1:9 (true light) and John 8:12 (light of the world); both cited. The ascription 'De eo namque Prophetae clamarunt' is plural in the print and kept as 'the prophets'.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 11, col. D, to p. 12, col. A (PDF pp. 35-36)

title: Why the angel first said “Hail, full of grace”
english: Fittingly, then, the Angel announced first of all to the holy Virgin Mary that word: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you (Luke 1:28), since the whole treasure of grace was stored up with her. For of all the generations this Virgin alone was holy in body and in spirit (1 Corinthians 7:34), and she alone carries Him who carries all things by His word (Hebrews 1:3). And it is not only the beauty of that most holy one in body that fills us with wonder, but also the virtues of her soul.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, cols. A-B (PDF p. 36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'sancta corpore et spiritu' matches the Vulgate of 1 Corinthians 7:34, said of the unmarried virgin; cited. 'qui verbo omnia portat' matches Hebrews 1:3 ('portansque omnia verbo virtutis suae'); cited. 'praesignificavit' with 'primo omnium' rendered 'announced first of all'. Margin variant 'al. Archangelus' not adopted. 'cum ipsa' and 'eum' are read from the page image, where c and e look alike in this typeface.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, cols. A-B (PDF p. 36)

title: The Lord is with you, not an earthly bridegroom
english: Therefore with those words, Hail, full of grace, the Angel first greeted her and addressed her: The Lord is with you (Luke 1:28). Not an earthly bridegroom, but the Lord of holiness Himself, the father of chastity, the author of incorruption and the giver of freedom; the one who brings about salvation, and the keeper and giver of true peace; who created man from the virgin earth (Genesis 2:7), and took Eve from his side and rib (Genesis 2:21-22): this Lord is with you, and in turn comes from you.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, cols. B-C (PDF p. 36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'sanctificationis Dominus' rendered 'the Lord of holiness'; the same choice is used for sanctificatio in section 13 (margin variant 'al. sanctitatis', 'holiness', gives the same sense). 'pater castitatis' kept lower-case, as in the print: a title of the Lord, not the First Person. 'ex terra virgine creavit hominem' alludes to Genesis 2:7 (Adam from untilled earth) and 'ex illius latere ac costa Evam' to Genesis 2:21-22; both cited. 'rursum ex te' rendered 'in turn comes from you'. Margin variant 'al. protulit, creavit' at 'assumpsit' not adopted.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, cols. B-C (PDF p. 36)

title: Let us join the angel's greeting
english: Come then, beloved, and let us too, following the angel's praise, pay as far as we are able the debt of thanks, saying: Hail and rejoice, full of grace, the Lord is with you (Luke 1:28). For it is truly yours to fare well and to rejoice, since divine grace, as it knows how, has chosen its dwelling with you: with the handmaid, the King of glory; with the beautiful one, He who is fair in form beyond the sons of men (Psalm 45:2); with the undefiled, He who sanctifies all things. With you is God, and from you is God, and perfect man, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells (Colossians 2:9).
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, cols. C-D (PDF p. 36); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 44' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 44:3 = Psalm 45:2 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. 'in quo omnis plenitudo divinitatis inhabitat' quotes Colossians 2:9; cited. 'Tuum ... est avere, atque gaudere' plays on Ave (from avere, 'to fare well'); rendered 'to fare well and to rejoice'. 'Rex gloriae' may recall Psalm 24:7-10 and 'ancilla' Luke 1:38; stock titles here, not cited. 'debitum ... grati' rendered 'the debt of thanks' (margin 'al. grato animo', 'with a grateful heart', gives the same sense).
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, cols. C-D (PDF p. 36)

title: Hail, full of grace: fountain, flower, meadow, vine, field
english: Hail, full of grace, fountain of light that enlightens all who believe in Him. Hail, full of grace, dawning of the spiritual Sun, and spotless flower of life. Hail, full of grace, most fragrant meadow. Hail, full of grace, ever-flourishing vine, who gladden the souls of those who glorify you. Hail, full of grace, field that bears the fairest fruits without being ploughed.

Your bearing was according to nature, in that you brought forth in our manner, keeping the time of the child's stirring and of carrying; but beyond nature, or rather above nature, because the divine Word came from on high and in your holy womb formed Adam anew. The Holy Spirit gave the holy Virgin her fruitfulness; but the true body was taken from her body.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 12, col. D, to p. 13, col. A (PDF pp. 36-37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Second paragraph opens 'Your bearing was according to nature' to carry the elliptical 'Secundum naturam quidem ... protulisti' as a full sentence; it supplies no new idea beyond protulisti. 'tempore motus, gestationisque servato' (as printed) rendered 'keeping the time of the child's stirring and of carrying'; 'the child's' makes explicit what motus means here (the sense of motus here is uncertain). 'quidem ... autem' pairs fecunditatem with corpus, so 'verum' is taken as the adjective ('the true body'), not as the conjunction 'but'. 'intelligibilis solis oriens' rendered 'dawning of the spiritual Sun' (intelligibilis = known by the mind, not the visible sun); the partly legible margin variant ('solis iustitiae'?) not adopted. 'fons lucis, qui ... illuminat' keeps the print's third person; 'in ipsum' = Christ. No Scripture cited: the titles are the author's own images.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 12, col. D, to p. 13, col. A (PDF pp. 36-37)

title: Like the pearl, Christ is born of the Virgin
english: And as the pearl comes from two natures, namely lightning and water, arising through certain hidden tokens and signs of the sea, so too our Lord Jesus Christ comes forth, without confusion and without change, from the pure and chaste, undefiled and holy Virgin Mary. He is perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, like the Father in all things and consubstantial with us in all things, but without any sin (Hebrews 4:15).
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, cols. A-B (PDF p. 37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'nobis per omnia consubstantialis, sed omnis peccati expers' echoes Hebrews 4:15 ('tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin'); cited. The two-natures formula (inconfuse, immutabiliter, perfect in Godhead and manhood, consubstantial with us) is post-Chalcedonian language and supports the later dating noted in the book's description. 'patri per omnia similis' confirmed on the page image (printed p. 13 col. A; lower-case 'patri' as the print writes 'pater' throughout). 'consubstantialis' kept as the exact doctrinal term 'consubstantial'. 'occultis quibusdam indiciis ac signis maris provenit' rendered close to the letter ('arising through certain hidden tokens and signs of the sea'; maris goes with signis); the sense is the ancient belief that pearls form from lightning striking the sea. The margin note on Ephrem's sermon on the pearl is an editor's cross-reference and was not translated.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, cols. A-B (PDF p. 37)

title: What prophets longed to see came to Mary alone
english: Many of the holy fathers, patriarchs, and prophets longed to see Him and to become eyewitnesses, and could not (Matthew 13:17; Luke 10:24). Some of them saw Him in visions, dimly and in riddles; others heard the divine voice in the pillar of cloud (Psalm 99:7) and were granted the sight of holy angels. But to Mary alone, the holy Virgin, the Archangel Gabriel came in clear light, announcing to her: Hail, full of grace (Luke 1:28). And so she received the Word, and in the time of bodily fulfilment she brought forth the precious Pearl.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, cols. B-C (PDF p. 37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'desiderarunt eum videre ... et non potuerunt' echoes Matthew 13:17 / Luke 10:24; cited. 'in columna nubis divinam vocem audierunt' matches the Vulgate of Psalm 98:7 ('in columna nubis loquebatur ad eos'), which is Psalm 99:7 in English Bibles; English numbering cited (compare Exodus 33:9). 'adumbratim in aenigmatibus' may recall Numbers 12:8 or 1 Corinthians 13:12; uncertain, not cited. 'Patrum' rendered lower-case 'fathers' (the Old Testament fathers, not God the Father). 'Pearl' capitalised as a title of Christ, continuing section 11. Margin variants 'al. in aenigmate' and 'al. Angelus' not adopted.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, cols. B-C (PDF p. 37)

title: Arise, Lord: the Virgin is the ark
english: Come then, you too, beloved, and let us sing those sweet words set before us from the spiritual harp of David, saying: Arise, O Lord, into Your resting place, You and the ark of Your holiness (Psalm 132:8). For truly the most holy Virgin is an ark, gilded within and without (Exodus 25:11), who received the whole treasure of holiness. Arise, O Lord, into Your resting place (Psalm 132:8). Arise, O Lord, from the bosom of the Father (John 1:18), to raise up the fallen race of the first parent.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, cols. C-D (PDF p. 37); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 131' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 131:8 = Psalm 132:8 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. The Latin 'arca sanctificationis tuae' is translated from the sermon's text ('ark of Your holiness'), not from the Hebrew-based English ('ark of Your might'). 'intrinsecus et extrinsecus deaurata' alludes to the ark overlaid with gold inside and out (Exodus 25:11); cited. 'ex sinu Patris' takes its phrase from John 1:18; cited. sanctificatio rendered 'holiness', as in section 8.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, cols. C-D (PDF p. 37)

title: David's prophecy: Hear, O daughter
english: Asking and pleading for this, David spoke in prophecy to the rod that was to put forth from him the flower of that most beautiful fruit (Isaiah 11:1), and said: Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father's house; and the King will desire your beauty, for He is the Lord your God, and you will worship Him (Psalm 45:10-11). Hear, O daughter, the things foretold of you before, so that you may also behold the realities themselves with the eyes of knowledge. Hear me, who signify them to you beforehand, and hear the Archangel, who plainly announces to you the mysteries fulfilled.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 13, col. D, to p. 14, col. A (PDF pp. 37-38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margin 'Psal. 44' is Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 44:11-12 = Psalm 45:10-11 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. The rod that puts forth a flower is Isaiah 11:1 (Vulgate 'egredietur virga de radice Iesse et flos de radice eius ascendet'); cited here and in section 15. 'rex' capitalised as King because the verse goes on 'He is the Lord your God'. 'in te praedicta' rendered 'foretold of you'. 'perfecta mysteria' rendered 'the mysteries fulfilled' (perfectus as accomplished). The faint margin note at 'adorabis eum' ('al. dele...'?) was not used.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 13, col. D, to p. 14, col. A (PDF pp. 37-38)

title: Let us praise the rod from Jesse
english: Come then, dearly beloved, and let us too, calling to mind what has gone before, glorify that rod from Jesse that blossomed so wonderfully and beyond all telling (Isaiah 11:1). Let us praise it together, call it blessed, and welcome it with joyful acclamations.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, col. A (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'virgam ... ex Iesse ... germinantem' alludes to Isaiah 11:1; cited. 'beatam praedicemus' may echo Luke 1:48 ('all generations will call me blessed'); possible, not cited. The rod (virga, feminine) stands for Mary; 'it' keeps the image as the print has it.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 14, col. A (PDF p. 38)

title: Luke's witness: the birth at Bethlehem
english: For Luke, bearing witness in the divine Gospels not to Joseph alone but also to Mary the Mother of God, and looking to the very family and kindred of David, tells the story and says: And Joseph also went up from Galilee to a city of Judea called Bethlehem, to be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was with child, because they were of the house and family of David (Luke 2:4-5). And it happened that while they were there, the days were fulfilled for her to give birth; and she brought forth her son, the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15), and wrapped Him in cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn (Luke 2:6-7).
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, cols. A-B (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margins 'Luc. 2', 'Ibidem': Luke 2:4-7. 'primogenitum omnis creaturae' is the author's blend of Luke 2:7 ('firstborn son') with Colossians 1:15 ('firstborn of all creation'); rendered once as 'her son, the firstborn of all creation' and cited to Colossians 1:15 beside the clause. The print puts the Bethlehem clause before 'because they were of the house ... of David'; that order is kept. 'Dei genitrix' rendered 'Mother of God' (Theotokos). Margin variant 'al. solum' at 'soli' not adopted. 'pannis' rendered 'cloths' to keep it distinct from 'fasciis' ('swaddling bands') in section 17.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Latin column, In annuntiationem Sermo I, printed p. 14, cols. A-B (PDF p. 38)

title: The Creator wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger
english: She swathed in swaddling bands Him who clothes Himself with light as with a garment (Psalm 104:2). She wrapped in cloths Him who formed all creation. She laid in a manger Him who sits above the cherubim (Psalm 80:1) and is praised by countless angels (Daniel 7:10). In the manger of beasts without reason the divine Word rested, to give a sense of reason to men who were truly without reason by their own free will. On the table of beasts of burden the heavenly bread was set out, to make men, who were without reason like cattle, sharers in the mystical food.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, cols. B-C (PDF p. 38); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: Margins 'Psal. 103' and 'Psal. 79' are Vulgate numbering: Vulgate Psalm 103:2 = Psalm 104:2 and Vulgate Psalm 79:2 = Psalm 80:1 in English Bibles; English numbering cited. Margin 'Dan. 7': Daniel 7:10 (thousands upon thousands serving Him). 'Fasciis eum' read for the print's 'Fasciis cum' (an evident misprint: the verb needs an object, and the next two sentences repeat 'eum'). The wordplay irrationalis / rationalis is kept as 'without reason' / 'a sense of reason'. 'redderet' has no expressed subject (the Word or the bread, which here is Christ); an infinitive of purpose ('to make') keeps that open. 'caelestis panis' may recall John 6:51 and 'instar pecorum' Psalm 49:12 (Vulgate 48:13); uncertain, not cited. Margin variant 'al. panis vitae appositus est' not adopted.

title: No room for Him who made heaven and earth
english: And there was not even room for them in the inn (Luke 2:7). He who built heaven and earth by His word (Genesis 1:1) had no place. For though He was rich, for our sake He became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), choosing the utmost lowliness for the salvation of our nature, out of the goodness toward us that is His by nature.

translator_notes: Margins 'Gen. 1' and '2. Cor. 8': creation by the word (Genesis 1, cited at 1:1 for 'heaven and earth') and 2 Corinthians 8:9. The opening sentence repeats Luke 2:7; cited. 'ingenita sua ... bonitate' rendered 'the goodness toward us that is His by nature' (ingenitus = inborn, innate). Creation by the word may also recall Psalm 33:6; not cited separately.

title: In the Father's bosom and in His mother's arms; closing doxology
english: He who carried out the whole providence and ordering of the hidden mysteries of the dispensation, in heaven in the bosom of the Father and in the cave in His mother's arms, rested in the manger. Choirs of angels surrounded Him, singing glory in heaven and announcing peace on earth (Luke 2:13-14). In heaven He sat at the right hand of the Father; and in the manger He rested as upon the cherubim. Truly this too was a throne of the cherubim, a royal throne: the holy of holies, alone glorious upon earth, holier than the holy, in which Christ our God rested.
To Him be glory, honor, and dominion, with the all-pure Father and the most holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
notes_covered: Vossius 1684 Latin column, printed p. 14, col. D, to p. 15, col. A (PDF pp. 38-39); Greek column OCR damaged
translator_notes: 'gloriam ... pacem' alludes to the angels' song in Luke 2:13-14; cited. 'a dextris Patris sedebat' is stock creedal language (compare Psalm 110:1; Hebrews 1:3) and 'super Cherubim' recalls Psalm 80:1, cited in section 17; neither cited again here. 'in sinu Patris' recalls John 1:18, cited in section 13. The sentence 'Qui ... implevit ... in praesepio requievit' has two verbs on one relative; rendered as one sentence with 'He who carried out ... rested in the manger', the two 'in heaven ... in the cave' phrases standing between them as in the Latin. 'Thronus ... et hic erat' taken with hic as the pronoun ('this too was a throne'); 'here too' would also fit. 'immaculatissimo Patre' rendered 'the all-pure Father'. 'in spelunca' (the cave of the Nativity) is the author's, not Luke's. 'super' and 'in quo' are damaged in the print (printed p. 15) and are supplied from the visible letters; the margin variant 'al. occulto dispensationis mysterio' not adopted.
